_comment: Replace every occurrence of markdown.example.edu with your own host. Nothing here is a
secret: the developer key's client id and secret are generated by Canvas when you paste
this in, and the tool's public key is fetched from public_jwk_url.
See docs/installation/canvas-self-hosted.md for where each value comes from, and
docs/research/canvas-lti-file-menu.md for why the configuration looks the way it does.
This key is ignored by Canvas; it exists so the file explains itself.
title: Markdown Viewer
description: Displays Markdown files stored in Canvas.
_comment_scopes: Empty on purpose. This tool calls no LTI Advantage service: it reads files through the
Canvas REST API with each user's own OAuth2 token, which is granted by a separate API
developer key. Asking for LTI scopes here would request access the tool does not use.
The API developer key needs exactly two scopes, both read-only:
Canvas publishes scopes for /api/v1 and /api/sis routes only, so the web download route
has none. The content is fetched through the url the File object itself supplies.

_comment_privacy: `public` lets Canvas send the user's name and email. The tool neither stores nor
logs them, and works identically with `anonymous`, which is the setting to prefer
if your institution would rather not send them at all.

_comment_accept_media_types: Canvas shows this placement only for files whose stored MIME type matches one
of these. The list is broad on purpose: Canvas records whatever the uploader's
browser claimed and only falls back to its own table when that is unusable, so
the same .md file may be stored as text/markdown, text/plain or
application/octet-stream depending on the machine it came from.
MEASURE YOUR OWN INSTANCE before narrowing this. Upload a .md file from the
browsers your users actually use and read back the `content-type` from
GET /api/v1/courses/:id/files. Narrowing it too far makes the menu entry vanish
for legitimate files; the tool validates the type again on the server either way.
Note also that Canvas applies this filter in the browser only: nothing enforces
it server-side, so it is a convenience, never a security control.
_comment_custom_fields: Canvas does not tell an LTI 1.3 tool which file the menu was opened from — see
